opener.heading: Week 7: Love & Friendship 💌
about: Everything Azlyn makes this week has somebody's name on it. Bread for next door on Friday, a Danish letter signed with dots instead of a name on Saturday, eight crooked cards on Sunday, a necklace measured against a real neck on Monday. The mailbox goes up by the front door on the first day and stays shut until Thursday, when she tips six days of mail onto the floor, sorts it into piles and walks it round the street herself.

Valentine's Day lands on the Sunday and gets the full day: hearts torn by hand, cards she glues without your help, and a table she sets for everyone in the house. Presidents' Day on Monday means a busier duck pond and not much else. The rest of the week runs on paper, flour and tape.
azlyn: Fine-motor work with a point to it. Threading forty pasta tubes, folding and snipping paper lace, buttering a whole slice of bread.
Counting that changes the outcome. Three stamps on a parcel, one plate per person, five dots for the five letters in her name.
Choosing for somebody else. She names the recipient first, then works out what that person would like, which is hard at three and gets easier with practice.
Handling food she has opinions about. Kneading dough, tearing lettuce, peeling clementines, cutting cucumber into sticks with a blunt knife.
Waiting when the wait is visible. A timer set for 9:15, a dough that rises on its own schedule, a mailbox that stays shut until Thursday.
you: Waiting for dough to rise is a better lesson than the bread
Celebrating other people's holidays does something specific
Ugly is fine. Ugly is better
Seeing the finish line is what builds persistence
Handling food is how picky eating loosens
Pretend play is where numbers stop being recitation
Naming the recipient at the start changes the whole activity
shopping: Thick card, 1 sheet, for the post office sign
Shoeboxes with lids, 2 (the mailbox Friday, the register Wednesday)
A small box for the real parcel
Old magazines and junk mail, a stack
Brown paper, or a big paper bag to cut open
Envelopes, 8, plus one old one to cut stamps from
Washable poster paint and a fine brush (if the spoon gets painted)
Heavy scissors or a craft knife (adult only)
Bread flour, 500 g, plus extra for the table
Butter, and cream cheese, a small tub
A dried herb, and jam, for the two dips
A lettuce or a bag of salad
All-purpose flour, butter, sugar, currants and an egg for the Welsh cakes
A jam jar for the table centerpiece
A tray or a basket, to carry the picnic through
A pitcher and a small cup per person
A blanket or a big towel for the floor
Silverware and a plate for everyone at Sunday dinner
Two washcloths you can get wet
A kitchen scale, or a coat hanger and 2 yogurt cups
A real coin to draw round, and change for the store and the post office
A candle in a stable holder, or a battery tealight
An old bed sheet or blanket
6 books she can carry from one room to another
A shopping bag or a basket
The postal address for Wednesday's parcel, written out large
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 8 months this week. He crawls or shuffles after whatever he wants, bangs two things together on purpose, and turns his face into your shoulder when a stranger leans over the stroller.

days.title: Bread for Next Door
days.prepTonight: Mix the bread dough tonight (flour, yeast, salt, sugar, warm water, oil), knead it for five minutes, cover the bowl and leave it in the fridge to rise overnight.

schedule.name: The Dough That Has to Wait

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: Rolls for the People Next Door

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath and the Book About Friends

opening.title: The Dough That Has to Wait
opening.need: the risen dough in its bowl, or a bought pack out of the fridge · extra flour · a timer · an envelope and a pen.
steps: Take the bowl of last night's dough out of the fridge and set it on the table in front of her. Lift the cloth and let her press one finger in. The dent stays where she put it.
Ask how many rolls she thinks are in there. Write her number on the back of the envelope and prop it against the bowl.
Flour the table and set the timer for 9:15. The dough is warming up and nobody touches it until the timer goes. She will check it four times.

main.title: Rolls for the People Next Door
materials: A 500 g pack of ready-made dough covers all five, if the bowl never got mixed
steps: Tip the dough onto the floured table and let her drive both fists into it until it goes back down to the size it started. This is the loud part and it lasts as long as she wants.
Cut it into twelve pieces. She rolls each one under a flat palm into a ball. The lumpy ones bake the same as the round ones.
Six to a lined tray, two fingers apart, dish towel over the top. Somewhere warm for forty minutes.
While they proof she draws on the two paper bags. Say the neighbors' names out loud so she knows where each bag is going.
Oven at 425°F. Bake fifteen minutes, until the tops are brown and the bottom of one sounds hollow when you knock it. Out around 10:25.
Three warm rolls into each bag at snack time. She eats one of the other six while she loads them.
main.tip: Count the finished rolls against the number on the envelope before they go in the oven.

outside.title: Delivering While It's Still Warm
paras: Coats on over the flour. Go while the paper is still warm, next door first and the second house after. She carries both bags herself. She knocks, she holds the bag out, she says who made them. February wind pulls the heat out of bread in about ten minutes, so knock on both doors first and do the rest of the walk afterwards.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and bangs two things together on purpose now, so give him a wooden spoon and an upturned plastic bowl on the kitchen floor while the rolls prove. On the doorstep, hold him facing you. Stranger wariness lands hard around eight months, and a neighbor leaning in gets a shoulder and a hidden face.

second.title: The Mailbox by the Door
second.intro: Everything Azlyn makes this week needs somewhere to go until Thursday. The mailbox goes up by the front door this afternoon.
materials: 1 cereal box or shoebox with a lid
Heavy scissors or a craft knife (adult only)
A bulldog clip or more tape to hang it
steps: Cut the slot in the lid: a long rectangle wide enough for a folded sheet and her whole hand. Your job, with her holding the far end steady.
Tape the lid on all the way round so the slot is the only way in.
Cover the box in paper and hand her the crayons. Every side is hers. Ask what a mailbox needs written on it and write down her words.
Hold it against the wall by the front door and let her say when the height is right. Tape or clip it there.
First delivery: she draws one thing for each person in the house, folds them, posts them. Nobody looks.
Say the rule out loud once: it stays shut until Thursday, and anything she makes for Thursday goes in it. Some things go straight to somebody's door the same day, and you say which.
Mark Thursday on the calendar and count the days with her.
second.tip: Hang it low. A mailbox she has to ask for help with turns into your mailbox by Sunday.

alternatives: A paper bag taped to the wall does the same job in four minutes.
One card for one person, posted through their real door instead.
Sort the junk mail into a pile for everyone in the house.
outAgain: A café, cake and a window to watch the street through
The corner store for a book of stamps, and she hands the money over
Back to the neighbor's, if the door opened and the kettle went on
The playground, if a morning at the table has left her wound up

aroundWorld.title: Wales and the Love Spoon 🥄
paras: In Wales a young man carved a wooden spoon for the person he was courting and handed it over as a way of saying so without saying it. The symbols carry the message: a heart for love, a key for a home, a chain for years together, beads for children. They hang on kitchen walls now.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Make Welsh cakes. Rub butter into flour and sugar, add currants and an egg, roll out, cut rounds and cook them on a dry pan for three minutes a side. Azlyn cuts the rounds.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: The oldest Welsh love spoon anyone has found is dated 1667.

days.krestonPM: He is crawling now and the floor belongs to him, so give him the offcut lid and a crumpled sheet of the covering paper, both too big for his mouth. At the café keep him in the carrier facing you. At eight months a stranger's face over the stroller gets a reaction, and he settles faster with yours in front of him.

insight.headline: Waiting for dough to rise is a better lesson than the bread.
paras: Azlyn spent an hour this morning with something she wanted to touch and could not, and she managed it. Children hold out longer when the wait has a visible marker (a timer, a bowl on the table, a dent that stays) and when the adult who set the terms has kept them before. Researchers who repeated the marshmallow test found that children waited far longer for the second treat when the adult had already kept one promise to them. You said 9:15 and you meant 9:15, so the next wait costs her less. Yeast is a good teacher because it cannot be hurried by anyone.

days.safety: The oven is on and the trays come out at her head height. Say so out loud every time you open the door, and keep Kreston out of the kitchen while trays are moving. Raw dough and hot rolls go where he cannot reach them. The craft knife goes back on a high shelf between cuts.

days.title: A Letter from Denmark
days.prepTonight: Put five sheets of white paper, the child-safe scissors and a pencil on the table, and check whether the envelope you want to use is somewhere you can find at eight in the morning.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Silver Buds on the Willow

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Paper Lace in the Window

opening.title: The Practice Snowflakes
steps: Fold a sheet in half, then in half again. Show her the folded corner and tell her that corner is the middle of the paper.
She snips lumps out of the folded edges. Do not pencil any guidelines on it.
Open it out together. Do two more and let her work out that snipping the folded edge makes the holes. The fourth sheet is the real one and it happens at 9:15.

main.title: The Letter Nobody Signs
main.intro: Danish children send a gækkebrev in the weeks before Easter: paper lace, a rhyme, and dots instead of a name.
materials: 1 envelope, or a sheet folded and taped shut
steps: Fold the good sheet in half and in half again, the way she practiced at 8:00. She snips it, you keep your hands off it.
Open it out flat and look at it in the window before you write on it.

Ask her what the letter should say and write her rhyme in the middle of the lace. If she stalls, offer her the shape and let her fill it: I made this, I made this thread, guess my name and get the bread. Take whatever she gives you.
Count the letters in her name on your fingers. Five. She draws five dots along the bottom of the letter.
Color the lace if she wants it colored. Fold it into the envelope and seal it.
It goes on the walk to the neighbors who got the bread yesterday, with nobody's name on the front.
main.tip: The dots are the whole game. Let her tell three people that the letter is secret.

outside.title: The Silver Buds on the Willow
paras: Pussy willows break in February and the buds come out gray and furry, which is the whole reason to walk to one. Look along a ditch, a damp corner of the park, the edge of a parking lot. Let her run a thumb over a bud before she looks at it. Drop the letter through their door on the way past, then take one twig with permission. A florist or the grocery store sells the cut branches all month if none grow near you.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months. Give him a sheet of parchment paper too big to go in his mouth and let him crush it with both hands, while the small snipped offcuts stay up on the table. Outside, hold a willow twig where he can swipe at it, and keep it in your own hand.

second.title: The Letters She Hides
second.intro: Three more letters, one for each person in this house, each hidden somewhere its owner has to find it.
materials: The morning's letter as the model
The willow twig or a green sprig from the walk
One small forfeit: a cookie or an extra bedtime story
steps: Fold and snip three letters. They come out faster now and better, which she will notice on her own.
Five dots along the bottom of each one. She counts them out loud every time.
Tape the willow twig or the sprig inside one of them, the way the Danish letters carry a flower.
Walk the house and pick the hiding places with her, every one of them above Kreston's reach: on top of the bookshelf, behind the kettle, on a shelf in the fridge. Let her choose the daft ones.
Set the terms before anybody hunts. Guess who sent it and Azlyn owes you a cookie. Guess wrong and you owe her one.
Send each person to find theirs. She watches the whole thing and gives no clues, which will take everything she has.
Guessing happens at dinner. Pay the forfeits then, out loud, whoever won.
second.tip: Guess wrong on purpose once, then pay up in front of her. A rule that costs you something is a rule she believes in.

alternatives: One letter for Joseph, hidden in his shoe, and stop there.
Snip the offcuts into confetti and sweep it up together.
Tape the paper lace to the window and look through it at the light.
Draw round her hand five times and cut out the hands instead.
outAgain: A train ride, two stops out and two stops back, and she holds the tickets
The station platform on its own if the ride is too much today
A drive to the park with the willows along the water
The indoor play center, for a Saturday that has been quiet and indoors
The park with the long path, on the bikes
days.krestonPM: Take him on the train. At 8 months the window is the whole trip, and he tracks a passing fence post to the edge of his vision and hunts for it again. Sit him on your lap facing the glass. If the train car is full and somebody friendly leans in, turn him toward you without apologizing for him.

insight.headline: Celebrating other people's holidays does something specific.
paras: Azlyn is three, which is the age children start sorting people into groups and attaching feelings to the sorting. A Danish letter cut on your own table arrives before any of that hardens. She is doing a Danish thing with her own hands, and at three the doing is the version that sticks. The custom turns ordinary because she has one in her own hands, snipped by her, hidden by her. Keep them small and keep them practical, a letter, a loaf, a song, and the message underneath is that families elsewhere are families, getting on with their own ordinary week.

days.safety: A willow twig snaps into mouth-sized pieces. The one Kreston swipes at stays in your hand, and every hiding place today sits above his reach, the letter with the twig in it included. Snipped offcuts and paper confetti are mouth-sized too, so sweep the floor before he is down on it, and keep his parchment sheet whole. Scissors go back to you between letters.

days.title: The Wonky Valentines
days.prepTonight: Flatten two cereal boxes, cut eight rectangles and fold them into cards, and put out the junk mail, the glue stick and a wet washcloth.

opening.title: Hearts Torn by Hand
opening.need: old magazines and junk mail · a few sheets of red or pink paper.
steps: Fold a page in half and tear half a heart along the fold, no scissors and no pencil line. Open it.
Hand her the pile and let her tear. Yours will look like hearts, hers will look like tools and animals, and both go in the box.
Aim for twenty and stop when she stops. They supply 9:15 and this afternoon, so tear more than you need.

main.title: The Cards She Makes Herself
materials: Thin card or cereal-box card, 8 pieces folded in half
The torn hearts from this morning
1 glue stick, or flour-and-water paste in a saucer
1 marker for the words she dictates
Old magazines or junk mail to tear up
steps: Line the eight blank cards up and ask her who each one is for. Write the name on the back of each one.
She glues. Hearts upside down, hearts over the edge, four hearts on one card and none on the next. Keep your hands in your lap.
Crayons after the glue. She scribbles across the hearts and it is meant to look like that.
Card by card, ask what it should say. Write down what comes out, word for word, and sign it with her name in her own attempt at letters.
Anything she wants to add after you have written on it goes on. The card is finished when she says it is.
Stack them by the mailbox. Half go in it now, half get handed over in person this afternoon.
main.tip: You will want to straighten one heart. Sit on your hands. She can see the difference between what she made and what you made.

outside.title: The Hunt for Red Things
paras: Cold and bright, and everything outdoors in February is brown, so red carries a long way. Count what you find: a mailbox, a front door, holly berries and rose hips on the stems, brake lights, somebody's scarf, a red car. The berries and the hips stay on the stems, because those two make a small child sick. On the way home she names the reddest thing on the street and tells you why.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and holds one thing in each hand while looking at a third. Give him a red burp cloth and a red plastic lid wider than his mouth on the floor near the gluing, and he will bang one on the other. Keep the torn scraps up on the table. Outside, hold a red leaf where he can see it in the stroller.

second.title: The Table She Decorates
second.intro: She dresses the table before anybody eats at it. Everything on it is hers to place, including who sits where.
materials: The leftover torn hearts, plus more paper
1 jam jar and whatever is growing outside
1 candle in a stable holder, or a battery tealight
steps: Tape the string flat along the front edge of the table, pulled taut, with a tab of tape every hand's width so no loop hangs down. She clips the hearts along it, and spacing is hers, so expect eleven at one end.
One torn heart per person becomes a place card. She writes the names, you write them underneath in small letters.
She decides who sits where and puts the cards down. Do not move them, even the one that puts Kreston at the head of the table.
Fold the napkins into triangles and let her do the second half. Triangles are hard at three and she gets better inside ten napkins.
Fill the jam jar outside: bare twigs, pine, a sprig of something evergreen. February gives you a green centerpiece and no flowers. The jar stands at the far end of the table, out of Kreston's reach.
Silverware last, one setting at a time, walking round the table with a fistful.
Light the candle at six, in front of her, and put it in the middle where nobody can knock it.
second.tip: Take a photo of the table before anyone sits at it. She sees the whole thing at once in the picture.

alternatives: Place cards only, no garland, and let the rest go.
Draw round every plate on paper and make paper placemats.
Set the table for the teddies on the floor instead.
outAgain: A long walk with the stroller, the whole loop, and hand out the other four cards on the way
The duck pond, if the far path is not too churned up
A drive to somebody's house to deliver a card at the door
The woods loop, for greenery for the jam jar
days.krestonPM: Give him a napkin. At 8 months, cloth that disappears and comes back is a joke he understands, so drop it over your face and let him pull it off, again, and again. At dinner he sits at the table with his own place card.

insight.headline: Ugly is fine. Ugly is better.
paras: Eight cards, no straight lines, and a heart glued half off the edge. The version where you tidied them would look better on the mantel and would teach her something you would rather she did not learn, which is that her work arrives at an adult for correction. A child who owns the whole job comes back to it on her own. Straighten one heart for her and she notices, and the next card gets handed to you before she has started it. She knows which marks are hers. Hand the wonky ones over as they are and let the people receiving them see her handwriting.

days.safety: A lit candle sits in the middle of the table, out of arm's reach of a high chair, and it goes out before anyone leaves the room. A battery tealight does the job if that sounds like work tonight. The garland runs at Kreston's standing height, so it stays taped flat and taut with no loop hanging anywhere, and it comes down at bedtime. Loose string at toddler height is a strangulation risk.

days.title: The Long Necklace
days.prepTonight: Dye the pasta: 200g of tubes split between three freezer bags, a tablespoon of vinegar and a squeeze of food coloring in each, shake, then spread on a lined tray to dry overnight.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Necklace with a Finish Line

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Lifting the Ice Off the Puddles

opening.title: Marking Where It Ends
opening.need: 1 shoelace or a length of string · clear tape · 1 large bead or a fat knot.
steps: The shoelace is the string for the pasta necklace she threads at 9:15. Ask who it is for, anybody in the house except Kreston, and say why. Hold the lace round that neck, loose, and let her see where the two ends meet.
Tie the finish knot there, or thread the big bead on and knot it in place. Everything she threads today goes in front of that mark.
Wrap the other end tight in tape until it is stiff as a shoelace tip.

main.title: The Necklace with a Finish Line
materials: Dried pasta tubes, 200g, dyed the night before, or plain undyed tubes, which thread the same
1 tbsp vinegar and a freezer bag per color (night before)
1 shoelace, or string with one end wrapped tight in clear tape
1 large bead or a fat knot as the finish marker
steps: Tip the dry pasta into three bowls by color and put the tray under her work so the runaways stay on the table.
Show her once: lace through the hole, out the other side, down to the knot. Then hand it over and stop demonstrating.
She threads. Say nothing about pattern for the first ten pieces. If she starts a repeat, name it out loud and leave it there.
Every few minutes, hold the lace up and show her the gap between the pasta and the knot.
Around forty pieces the gap closes. Tie the ends together with her finger holding the knot down, and cut the tape off.
She puts it round the neck she measured. Put your phone down and be in the room for it.
main.tip: A dropped piece rolls under the table and she will want to go after it. Hand her a spare from your pocket instead.

outside.title: Lifting the Ice Off the Puddles
paras: A February morning after a cold night leaves sheets of ice over puddles, the water gone from underneath. Slide a boot toe under the edge and lift a whole pane out. Hold it to the sky and look through it. Let her drop it, stamp on it, listen to it. A mild night leaves nothing to lift, so count the puddles instead and rank them by how far up her boot the water comes. Find the thickest lid on the street and come back tomorrow to see if it survived.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months. Make him a rattle while she threads: two dyed pasta tubes in an empty water bottle, lid taped on hard. He shakes it, bangs it and rolls it away, then goes after it, which is new this month. Outside, hold a shard of ice near him and let him touch it with one finger.

second.title: Jobs That Need Two People
second.intro: Every job this afternoon is impossible on your own. Holding one end turns out to be a job.
materials: 6 books to move from one room to another
1 dishpan with two inches of water and 2 cups
steps: The basket ride first. She sits in the laundry basket with the cushion and you tow it the length of the hall. Then she tows the teddies back.
The sheet. One corner each, walk it across the room without letting it touch the floor, then fold it walking toward each other.
The book relay. Six books from one room to another with a rule: she carries, you open doors, neither of you does both.
Sweeping. You hold the dustpan, she brushes into it, then swap and let her tell you what you missed.
Washing dishes in the dishpan on the floor with two cups. She washes, you dry, then swap. Water gets everywhere and the dish towel is for the floor.
Ask which job was easier with two people.
Finish with the basket again. Eighty minutes of work earns a ride.
second.tip: Do each job wrong on purpose once. Drop your corner of the sheet, miss the dustpan. Her fixing your end is worth more than her doing her end right.

alternatives: The basket ride and nothing else, up and down the hall until you give out.
Carry the laundry basket out to the clothesline together, one handle each.
Move every cushion in the house into one pile, two hands per cushion.
outAgain: The duck pond, busier than usual with everybody off for Presidents' Day
The neighborhood park, on the way back from the pond
The green space with a ball, if the ground is not frozen solid
A walk past this morning's puddle to see whether the ice came back
days.krestonPM: He comes on the basket rides on your lap and shouts for more. At 8 months he anticipates a repeat: pause at the top of the hall and he tenses up before you move. At the pond, hold him where he can watch the ducks land.

insight.headline: Seeing the finish line is what builds persistence.
paras: The knot on the lace is doing more work than the pasta. A three-year-old cannot hold an abstract goal in her head for forty minutes, so an unmarked string runs on forever and she wanders off at piece nine. Mark the end and the task turns into something she can watch herself win. Adults use progress bars and mile markers for the same reason: visible progress feeds the effort that produces more of it. She will start telling you how much is left. Use the finish-line trick on the jobs she hates too, and put a mark on the end of the tidying.

days.safety: Kreston is 8 months and crawling, and he can drown in the two inches of water in that dishpan, so it stays within your arm's reach while it is on the floor and gets tipped out the moment step 5 finishes. A long string necklace is a strangulation risk. It comes off for sleep, it never goes near Kreston, and it hangs on a hook overnight. Dried pasta on the floor is choking-sized for an 8-month-old who crawls toward whatever he sees, so sweep before he is down. A lifted ice pane snaps into mouth-sized pieces, so Kreston touches ice in your hands and never holds a piece of his own. The puddle you lift a pane off leaves a slick behind, so watch your footing there while you are carrying him.

days.title: The Lunch She Made
days.prepTonight: Put the four blunt table knives and the cutting board on the counter, stand the yogurt and the cream cheese at the front of the fridge, and find a blanket big enough for everyone to sit on.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Washing What Goes on the Plates

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: Plates for the People Who Live Here

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Tea Set and the Teddies

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Warm Bath After the Pool

opening.title: Washing What Goes on the Plates
opening.need: the cucumber, lettuce and clementines · 1 bowl of cool water · 1 dish towel.
steps: Bowl of water on the table, everything that needs washing beside it, dish towel across her lap.
She washes and dries each item and lines them up. Name each one as it comes out of the water.
Ask who is eating lunch today and count the names on her fingers. That number is how many plates she builds at 9:15.

main.title: Plates for the People Who Live Here
materials: 1 lettuce or a bag of salad
1 bowl of warm soapy water and a dish towel
steps: Butter first. Blunt knife, bread flat on the board, and let her go until the whole slice is covered even if it takes four minutes.
Cutting: cucumber into sticks rather than coins, cheese into strips, table knife, her hand on top of yours for the first three.
Tearing is where she is strongest, so give her the lettuce and the bread crusts to tear straight onto the plates.
Peeling the clementines is a fifteen-minute job at three. Start the skin with your thumbnail and hand it over.
One plate per person, side by side. She decides what goes on whose. Somebody is getting nine cucumber sticks and no bread.
Cover them and put them in the fridge until twelve. She carries them to the table herself at lunch and says whose is whose.
main.tip: Eat what she made in front of her, including the odd plate.

outside.title: Buying the One Missing Thing
paras: One thing lunch needs is not in the fridge. Walk to the store for it, no list and no cart. She carries the coins, finds it on the shelf, hands it over and takes the change. February sidewalks are wet and a ten-minute walk will take thirty, so leave early.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and eats lunch at the same table as everyone else. Give him his own plate with a long strip of banana and a soft strip of pear, both cut as long as his fist so a piece sticks out of the top. He rakes food toward himself and misses. Azlyn can make his plate too, with you checking the shapes.

second.title: The Picnic on the Floor
second.intro: Lunch was cold and served at the table. This one runs on the floor, and she is the one carrying it in.
materials: Plain yogurt, 4 tbsp, and cream cheese, 4 tbsp
A dried herb, and 1 tsp jam
The other half of the cucumber and whatever salad is left
1 blunt table knife and 1 cutting board
1 blanket or a big towel for the floor
1 tray or a basket to carry it through
1 pitcher of water and a small cup each
steps: She picks the room and spreads the blanket. Move whatever furniture she asks you to move.
Yogurt into one bowl, cream cheese into the other. She stirs the herb through the first and the jam through the second, tasting off a clean spoon after each stir.
She names each dip after whoever she thinks will like it most. Write those two names on strips of tape and stick them to the bowls.
Cucumber and salad onto the board and into sticks, blunt knife, her hand on top of yours for the first three.
Load the tray: bowls, sticks, crackers, cups, pitcher. She carries it through in two trips rather than one.
She lays a place for every person, sits Kreston beside her and serves. Take what she hands you and eat it where you are sitting.
Everything comes back to the kitchen on the tray. She takes the empty bowls and you take the pitcher.
second.tip: Let her taste both dips before anybody else does. She mixed them, so the first opinion in the room should be hers.

alternatives: The blanket and the crackers, and skip the dips.
One dip only, yogurt and jam, mixed and eaten off a spoon.
Picnic on the stairs, if the floor is under something else.
outAgain: Swimming
The pool's quiet session, if Tuesday afternoons are chaos right now
A warm bath at home with cups and pitchers, if the pool is shut
The library on the way home, half an hour before it shuts
days.krestonPM: He sits in the water against your chest, slaps the surface and watches the splash he made. Twenty minutes, then out before he cools. Hold him upright with his face level with yours so the pool noise arrives with something familiar in front of it.

insight.headline: Handling food is how picky eating loosens.
paras: Azlyn had her hands in food she has strong opinions about this morning, off and on, and nobody asked her to taste any of it. That is the useful part. Children who handle, tear, peel and serve unfamiliar food eat more of it later, and the route runs through touch and smell rather than through persuasion at the table. Making a plate for somebody else adds a second thing: she has to think about what Joseph likes, which puts her outside her own preferences for a minute. Keep tasting optional today. The cucumber she cut has a better chance tomorrow than the cucumber you cut.

days.safety: Cucumber coins, cheese rounds and whole grapes are choking-sized for Kreston at 8 months, so everything on his plate is cut into long strips. Blunt table knives only, and they go in the drawer before he is on the floor. The picnic runs at his height, so the crackers and the sticks stay on the tray in front of you and not loose on the blanket, and he skips the jam dip. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: The Post Office
days.prepTonight: Wrap six to ten small things in newspaper and tape them into parcels after she is in bed, and cut thirty stamps out of an old envelope.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Post Office on the Table

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Reading What She Chose at the Library

opening.title: Stamps, Coins and a Sign
opening.need: paper · 1 real coin · 1 marker · 1 sheet of card · scissors (yours).
steps: She draws round the real coin twenty times and you cut the circles out. Coins done.
Hand her the sheet of card and ask what the sign over the counter should say. Write her words, big, and let her color every letter in.
Tape the sign to the wall behind the kitchen table. The table is now a post office and it stays one until bedtime.

main.title: The Post Office on the Table
materials: 6–10 small parcels wrapped in newspaper and taped
A kitchen scale, or a coat hanger with a yogurt cup hanging from each end
30 paper stamps cut from an old envelope
20 paper coins drawn round a real coin and cut out
1 marker and 1 sheet of card for the sign
steps: Set the counter: the scale at one end, stamps and coins in the shoebox register, parcels in a heap on the customer's side. She stands behind, you line up in front.

Weigh the first parcel together and read the scale out loud. Turn whatever it says into a price between one and five and write it on the parcel in marker. With the coat hanger, count how many paper coins it takes to tip the pot and use that number.
The rule of the counter: the number on the parcel is how many stamps it needs and how many coins it costs. Say it once, then play it.
Buy a parcel. She counts the stamps out one at a time onto the paper and sticks them down, then counts your coins into the register.
Miscount on purpose. Hand over two coins for a three, and wait. She will catch it.
Swap. You run the counter, she stands in line with her coin purse.
main.tip: Weigh two parcels that look wrong: a big light one and a tiny heavy one.

outside.title: Counting the Front Doors
paras: Walk one street and count every front door you pass. Read out the numbers on them and let her spot the mailboxes, the ones by the door and the ones on posts. Count the red doors on the way back and compare the two numbers. Forty-five minutes is one street and back at her pace, so pick the short side of the block.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and paper coins are the size he should not have, so give him his own parcel: a scarf pushed into a box he can pull out and stuff back in. Hiding and finding is his whole project this month.

second.title: The Real Parcel
second.intro: This box has a real address on it and somebody waiting at the other end.
materials: Brown paper, or a paper bag cut open and turned inside out
Her drawings and letters from this week
The address written out large for her to copy from
steps: Decide who it goes to before anything goes in the box. Somebody real with a real address, and she names them.
Open the mailbox for the one thing she wants to send, then close it again. Everything else in there waits for Thursday.
Load the box: her drawings, a card from Sunday, a letter with dots on it. Let her crumple newspaper into the gaps and press it all down.
Wrap it in brown paper on the floor, her finger holding the fold while you tape. Corners are hard and hers will be lumpy and taped four times.
Put the address, written out large, beside her. She copies it onto the parcel with the marker. Wobbly, backwards, too big for the box, and it goes in the mail like that.
She draws in the space that is left over.
Stand it by the front door with the coats. It goes tomorrow morning and she needs to see it waiting.
second.tip: Write the address once, in capitals, one line under the other.

alternatives: Mail a card instead of a parcel and let her lick the stamp.
Wrap a shoebox in newspaper and mail it to somebody in this house.
Weigh everything in the kitchen cupboard and line it up lightest to heaviest.
outAgain: The library, every two weeks, and she chooses her own two books
The librarian's story hour, if the timing lands
The indoor play center, if the library is packed after school
The post office to see a real counter before tomorrow
days.krestonPM: Take him to the library and put him down in the board-book corner. At 8 months he crawls to the shelf he wants, pulls one out and chews the corner. Let Azlyn choose his and carry it to the desk. Hold him facing you at the counter. The librarian saying hello may not go down well this month.

insight.headline: Pretend play is where numbers stop being recitation.
paras: Behind a pretend counter Azlyn does arithmetic she will not do on request. The parcel needs three stamps, and three has a consequence: put two on and the customer complains, so she checks herself. Vygotsky watched this and wrote that a child in play behaves a head taller than herself, and a pretend counter is where you will see it happen. The frame does the work. Nobody is testing her. She is running a post office, and a clerk who miscounts finds out from the customer, which lands better than a correction from you. Play the customer with a straight face.

days.safety: Thirty paper stamps and twenty paper coins end up on the floor, and all of them are mouth-sized for a crawling 8-month-old. Sweep the floor before Kreston is down, and count the coins back into the register when the counter closes. Scissors and packing tape stay with you.

days.title: Delivery Day
days.prepTonight: Put the wooden spoon, the permanent markers and a scrap of ribbon on the table, and stand the wrapped parcel by the front door with the coats.

opening.title: Choosing Who It's For
steps: Tell her she is making one thing today and she chooses who gets it. Do not say what it is.
Write the name she gives you at the top of the paper. She sticks with it better once she can see it written down.
Ask one question about that person and write the answer underneath: something they like, or something she does with them. It comes back at 9:15.

main.title: The Wooden Love Spoon
main.intro: Welsh love spoons carry symbols instead of words.
materials: 1 plain wooden spoon (or a spoon shape cut from a cereal box)
Permanent markers, or washable poster paint and a fine brush
1 sheet of paper for practicing the four symbols
Masking tape for the name label
steps: Draw the four symbols on the practice paper and say what each means: heart for love, key for a home, knot for staying together, beads for the people in a family.
She copies each on paper first, twice. Hearts come out as blobs and keys as sticks, and both are fine.
Ask which symbols belong on this spoon, for this person. Take her reasons at face value even when the key is on there because the person has a car.
She draws them onto the bowl and the handle. Markers bleed on bare wood, so let the lines go fat.
Write the name she chose at 8:00 down the handle and let her trace over your writing.
Tie the ribbon round the neck of the spoon. Set it somewhere high to dry.
main.tip: Do a spoon yourself alongside her. She watches your hand more than your instructions.

outside.title: Mailing the Parcel
paras: The parcel by the door goes to a real post office this morning. She carries it in, hands it up to the counter, watches it go on the scale and hears the price. Buying the stamp is her job with your money. A gray February line is a long wait at three, so bring the practice paper and let her draw hearts in the line.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and works out who is safe by checking your face first. In the post office line he will look at each stranger, then back at you, then decide. Say the person's name out loud when somebody speaks to him and hold him where he can see your expression.

second.title: Emptying the Mailbox
second.intro: Six days of mail comes out on the floor at once.
materials: The mailbox from Friday and everything in it
Sticky labels or masking tape for names
steps: Take the box off the wall, sit on the floor with her and tip the lot out. Let her go through it before anyone sorts.
One pile per person. She decides where each card, letter and drawing belongs, and she will remember more of it than you expect.
Anything with no owner goes in a spare pile. Ask her at the end who those are for.
Fold each pile into an envelope, or a sheet of paper taped shut. She writes a name on every one, with the letters large beside her to copy.
The spoon goes in the basket with the envelopes. The necklace stays on the neck she measured it against on Monday.
Coats on and walk the round: next door, the house with the dog, the friend two streets over, whoever is on her list. She knocks and hands it over herself.
Anything undelivered comes home in the basket for tomorrow. No adult mails anything on her behalf tonight.
second.tip: Stand back on the doorstep. Let her be the one who talks, even when the neighbor looks at you for translation.

alternatives: Sort the piles and deliver two of them, not eight.
Photograph every piece before it leaves the house.
Keep one card back for the memory box.
Deliver to the people inside this house and stay indoors.
outAgain: The bakery, and she chooses buns for everyone by counting the people
The corner store for milk, with the change in her hand
One more delivery street, if the basket is still full
The park in the last of the light, for the running she has not done today
A friend's doorstep with the last envelope and a cup of tea if it is offered
days.krestonPM: He gets a pile too, and Azlyn will make sure of it. Sit him in the middle of the sorting. At 8 months he bangs two envelopes together, tears one and gets a fistful in his mouth, so stay next to him and swap the paper for a cloth book. In the carrier for the walk round, facing you.

insight.headline: Naming the recipient at the start changes the whole activity.
paras: Azlyn picked a person at 8:00 this morning before she knew what she was making, and the spoon came out better for it. Effort goes up when the work has a face attached: children this age stick with a task longer and take more care when a specific person is waiting at the other end of it, and the same thing shows up in adults. There is a second thing happening too. Deciding what somebody else would like is perspective-taking, which is hard at three and gets easier with practice on real people she can picture. The name first, then the making.

days.safety: A fistful of torn paper is a choking risk. Stay beside Kreston in the sorting pile and swap the paper for a cloth book the moment he starts tearing. Permanent markers stay capped and out of reach between symbols, and the spoon dries somewhere high. On the round she does the knocking and you stand within arm's reach of the curb.
